author: Hussain Nasser
headline: Venture building × AI × games in Saudi Arabia | PE & M&A modelling and valuation | Portfolio Manager, Revival Lab | Investment Director, Glo
text:
For every $100 of revenue in its latest quarter, Nvidia kept $66 as operating profit. Equinix kept $23. CoreWeave kept $6, then paid $23 in net interest.

So who keeps the margin in AI data centres: the chipmaker, the GPU cloud, or the landlord? I went through the latest filings. Three things stood out:

1. The chip layer keeps most of it. Nvidia's quarter to July: revenue $96.2B, data centre $89.0B, gross margin 75.0%. It guides 74% for the quarter to October.

2. The landlord earns a steady margin. Equinix's Q3 revenue was $2.57B, up 11%, with a 51% adjusted EBITDA margin. Bookings hit a record $533M, up 35%.

3. The GPU cloud in the middle gets squeezed. CoreWeave's Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin was 62%, above Equinix. After $1.89B of depreciation its operating margin was 6%, and net interest of $846M was about 23% of its $3.66B revenue, so it still posted a $709M net loss. It has a backlog of about $132.5B, so what it's short of is cheap capital.

For the Gulf, HUMAIN is building in the two thinner layers, the buildings and the GPU cloud. Its first 14 MW of Blackwell systems deploy from Q4 2026, and 70 MW of Vera Rubin is planned from mid-2027, 50 MW of it for a US client.

What it can work on are the two lines that hurt CoreWeave, power and capital. Saudi cloud operators pay 18 halalas per kWh (about $0.048), a tariff approved in 2021. HUMAIN's funding this year includes SAR 9.9B ($2.6B) in cash from Aramco and up to SAR 2.5B ($667M) of Infra facilities signed this week.

text:
Silver Lake and PIF reportedly discussed buying Unity at about $25B. No deal has been agreed.

That's about 16% above Unity's market cap, and about 24 times its annualised Q3 adjusted EBITDA of $257M.

Two things stand out in Unity's Q3:

1. Ads drive the growth. Grow Solutions rose 44% to $457M. Create, the engine, went to $165M from $152M.

2. Cash. Free cash flow was $220M. On a run-rate, that's about a 3.5% yield at $25B.

What I'll watch: whether Unity confirms a sale process.

Studio founders: do you see Unity more as an engine or an ads business?

Sources: Reuters via PocketGamer.biz and Enterprise AM; Unity Q3 2026 results (SEC filing)

author: Hussain Nasser
headline: Venture building × AI × games in Saudi Arabia | PE & M&A modelling and valuation | Portfolio Manager, Revival Lab | Investment Director, Glo
text:
Saudi startups raised $1B in the first nine months of 2026. Two deals made up 56% of it.

MAGNiTT's 9M figures, against the same period last year:

Funding: down 29%
Deals: 113, down 39%
Funding outside the two mega rounds: down 50%
Active investors: down 26%
International investor participation: down 51%

Two things I'd take from it:

1. Two rounds worth $563M carry the headline. Take them out and the rest of the market is back at 9M 2024 levels.

2. International investors pulled back the most. That leaves more of the work to local funds, and more depends on how steadily they deploy.

Series A held up better than the rest. Deal count there fell 17%, so companies with traction are still raising. Early-stage activity is where it softened.

For the next quarter I'll watch non-mega funding before the headline total.

Founders and fund managers here: does this match what you're seeing in your pipeline?

Sources: MAGNiTT Saudi Arabia 9M 2026 report, entARABI
#VentureCapital #GCC #SaudiArabia #VentureBuilding #Startups

comments.author: Pavel Shcherbakov
comments.text: If international investors cut their participation in half, the local lead now does the diligence they used to share. It's a lot of work: HBR's survey of 885 VCs (Gompers et al.) found a closed deal takes about 83 days and 118 hours of diligence on average. So next quarter the Series A money will go to companies that show up with the model, the data room and customer references ready.

comments.author: Muhammad Hasnain Pirzada
comments.text: Deals down 39 percent is the number that matters more than the headline. Fewer startups getting funded means the ones that do need to show real revenue earlier. Lean teams have the advantage now
